questions.q: What is the fix for the column-name-guessing failure seen in Lessons 45 and 46?
options: Paste the actual schema — real column names and types — before asking for code or an explanation
Never ask an LLM to write any code involving column names
Always use generic column names like col1, col2 in every prompt
Wait for the code to fail before providing any schema information
questions.explain: Giving schema context up front prevents the model from guessing at column names it has never actually seen.

questions.q: Why do sample rows matter in a documentation or code-generation prompt, beyond just column names?
options: Because column names alone underdetermine meaning — real values, including edge cases, disambiguate what a column actually represents
Because sample rows are required by every LLM's API
Because column names are never included in schemas
Because sample rows replace the need for any schema information
questions.explain: This is the same lesson from Lesson 48's total_amount example — the cancelled-order row was the evidence that disambiguated the column's real meaning.

questions.q: Why does asking for the model's reasoning, not just the final answer, matter for review?
options: A walked-through explanation is something you can check against your own understanding, while a bare answer must be trusted blindly or redone
Reasoning requests always produce faster responses
Reasoning is required for the model to run at all
Asking for reasoning removes the need for any further review
questions.explain: A one-line answer with no reasoning is hard to review — the reasoning is what turns output into something checkable.

questions.q: What does 'iterative refinement' mean as a prompting pattern?
options: Treating a prompt as a conversation — pointing out specifically what's wrong and letting the model revise, rather than writing one perfect prompt up front
Submitting the exact same prompt multiple times until it works by chance
Never revising a prompt once it has been submitted
Writing the longest possible prompt to avoid any follow-up
questions.explain: The first response rarely nails every constraint — pointing out specifics ('this misses the cancelled-order filter') and revising is faster than over-engineering one prompt.

questions.q: How do the four prompting patterns in this lesson relate to each other?
options: They compound: schema and sample rows improve the first draft, reasoning makes it reviewable, and iterative refinement fixes what review catches
They are mutually exclusive and only one can be used per prompt
They only apply to KQL and never to PySpark
They eliminate the need for any human review once combined
questions.explain: Lessons 45, 46, and 48 each used this same combination already — this lesson names the pattern explicitly so it's reusable on purpose.
